questions.question: What does errors.New do, and when do you use it?
questions.title: Rrors.new Do, And When Do You Use
questions.direct_answer: Creates a simple error value with a fixed message. Use when the error needs no data — just an identity.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Errors New beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Creates a simple error value with a fixed message. Use when the error needs no data — just an identity.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
errors.New takes a string and returns an error whose Error() method returns that string. That's all it does — but that gives you a value you can return, compare, and pass around, which is the whole error-as-value contract.

Use it when the error carries no payload: a fixed condition with a fixed meaning. 'queue is full', 'config missing' — states where a string fully describes the failure and no caller needs to extract fields from it. The moment an error needs data — which file, what status code, what retry-after — a string isn't enough, and you want a custom type or fmt.Errorf.

The other major use is sentinel errors: package-level vars like `var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")` that callers can match with errors.Is. Because the package exports one specific value, identity comparison works — the error is both the message and the key.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
What errors.New returns is worth looking at once. Historically it returned a *errorString — a pointer to a struct holding your string:

```go
type errorString struct { s string }
func (e *errorString) Error() string { return e.s }
```

Two consequences of the pointer:

First, two errors.New calls with identical text are different errors. errors.New("x") == errors.New("x") is false — separate allocations. Equality is identity, which is exactly what sentinel usage wants: only the one exported var matches.

Second, the Error() method on the pointer means errors.Is comparisons are pointer comparisons — cheap and exact. When Go 1.21 added errors.ErrUnsupported and friends, they were created with errors.New for exactly this identity semantics.

That's the whole mental model: errors.New is the minimal error — an identity plus a message, nothing more, ideal when 'which error' matters more than 'what details'.

questions.question: What is errors.New vs fmt.Errorf?
questions.title: Rrors.new Vs Fmt.errorf
questions.direct_answer: errors.New: fixed string. fmt.Errorf: formatted message; with %w it also wraps a cause for errors.Is/As. Use Errorf when you need context or values in the message.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: errors.New: fixed string. fmt.Errorf: formatted message; with %w it also wraps a cause for errors.Is/As. Use Errorf when you need context or values in the message.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
They overlap but serve different jobs. errors.New is the fixed case: one string, one error, no formatting. fmt.Errorf is the richer case: it builds the message from a format string and arguments, so the error can carry the specifics — the file name that failed, the URL that timed out, the index that was out of range.

```go
errors.New("could not open file")                    // fixed
fmt.Errorf("could not open %s: %w", path, err)      // context + cause
```

The second example shows the bigger difference: %w. When fmt.Errorf's format contains %w, the returned error records the wrapped error as unwrap-able — errors.Is and errors.As can walk through the new message into the original cause. %v would embed the cause's text but sever the chain. So the choice is really: no message assembly (errors.New), assembly without a cause (Errorf with %v), or assembly that preserves the cause for inspection (Errorf with %w).

Rule of thumb: errors.New for fixed identities and sentinels; Errorf whenever runtime values belong in the message; %w whenever the caller below you may need to match or extract the underlying error.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The %w vs %v difference is the interview-worthy part, because they print identically and differ only in what they preserve:

```go
base := errors.New("disk full")
withW := fmt.Errorf("write config: %w", base)
withV := fmt.Errorf("write config: %v", base)

errors.Is(withW, base)  // true — chain intact
errors.Is(withV, base)  // false — text only, no link
```

Both print as 'write config: disk full'. Only the %w version answers 'was the underlying cause disk full?' — because %w tells fmt.Errorf to store the cause in the error's Unwrap chain, and errors.Is walks that chain. With %v the cause's text is baked into the string at construction and the value itself is discarded.

That's why style guides settled on: wrap with %w when the caller might need the cause (most layers), use %v when the cause is genuinely only for humans (top-level log formatting), and reach for errors.New only when there's nothing to say beyond the identity.

questions.question: Can two errors.New with the same text be compared equal?
questions.title: Can Two Errors.new With The Same Text
questions.direct_answer: No. Each call creates a distinct value — equality is identity, not text. Compare with errors.Is against a shared sentinel.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: No. Each call creates a distinct value — equality is identity, not text. Compare with errors.Is against a shared sentinel.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
No — and this is by design. errors.New allocates a new error value each call; two of them with the same string have the same message but different identities. `errors.New("not found") == errors.New("not found")` is false. The == comparison on errors compares pointers, and the pointers differ.

If you need error equality, the pattern is the sentinel: create the error once at package level and let everyone compare against that one value.

```go
var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")

// both sides reference THE SAME value
if err == ErrNotFound { ... }            // works — identity match
if errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) { ... }   // also works, and survives wrapping
```

The errors.Is form is the modern one because it also matches when some layer wrapped the sentinel with %w — the identity is preserved through the chain. Raw == is fast but blind to wrapping, so Is is the default and == the optimization you make when you control both sides of the comparison.

The failure mode to avoid: matching by message text. `if err.Error() == "not found"` breaks the moment anyone edits a message — identity is stable, prose isn't.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why does identity work this way? Because the error interface is satisfied by a pointer type (*errorString), and interface values containing pointers compare by the pointer:

Two interface values are == when their dynamic types match AND their dynamic values are ==. For pointer types, value equality is pointer equality — same allocation. Two errors.New calls mean two allocations, two pointers, inequality. Same string inside is irrelevant.

This is precisely the property that makes sentinel errors reliable. If equality were text-based, then any error anywhere with the message 'not found' would match your sentinel — including ones that mean something subtly different. Identity restricts matching to the one value you deliberately created, and the package-exported var makes that value addressable for comparison.

The pattern generalizes: io.EOF, sql.ErrNoRows, fs.ErrNotExist — the standard library's sentinels are all single values, and the ecosystem matches them with errors.Is for exactly this reason. The identity isn't a quirk to work around; it's the feature.

questions.question: How do you define sentinel errors in Go?
questions.title: Efine Sentinel Errors In Go
questions.direct_answer: Package-level var: var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found"). Callers match with errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound). The single value is the identity.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Package-level var: var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found"). Callers match with errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound). The single value is the identity.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Deep Dive
sections.content:
What makes the sentinel reliable is a chain of small invariants:

1. errors.New returns a pointer — two calls are never equal (identity semantics).
2. The var is created once at package init — every return of ErrNotFound shares that one pointer.
3. errors.Is walks the Unwrap chain — wrapping the sentinel with %w preserves the match.
4. The Err prefix signals 'this is a value to compare against' at the call site.

Break any link and the pattern fails: create the error inside the function (new pointer each time — callers can never match), return a wrapped copy without %w (Is can't see through), or name it without the convention (callers miss it).

The alternative that eventually outgrows sentinels: typed errors with fields. sql.ErrNoRows tells you WHICH row was missing only by context; a *NotFoundError{Name: "users/42"} can carry it. The standard library uses sentinels where the condition is universal and types where details matter — a good calibration for your own APIs. Start with the sentinel; add a type when the caller needs more than 'this happened'.

questions.question: What is the downside of errors.New for caller-side decisions?
questions.title: Nside Of Errors.new For Caller-side Decisions
questions.direct_answer: A static string carries no data — callers can only match identity, not extract fields. Custom error types carry the details.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: A static string carries no data — callers can only match identity, not extract fields. Custom error types carry the details.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why is 'parse the message' so strongly forbidden? Because it couples the caller to your prose. The day the message becomes 'rate-limited, try in 30s' for tone, every string-matching caller silently breaks — no compile error, just a failed match at runtime that looks like a different error. Struct fields are a contract; strings are a convenience.

The deeper structure here: an error value's job is to let the caller branch correctly. Different branches need different information:

- 'Is this retryable?' → a Retryable() bool method, or a sentinel set membership
- 'What do I tell the user?' → a UserMessage() or typed codes
- 'What do I log/alert?' → the wrapped chain already carries it
- 'Which record failed?' → a field on the type

errors.New answers none of these beyond identity; fmt.Errorf with %w preserves the chain that does; a custom type with methods carries the answers directly. The standard library's os.PathError is the canonical middle step: it's a struct with Op, Path, and Err fields — a type, because 'which path failed' is the first thing every caller of file code asks. When your callers would ask a question the message can't answer structurally, you've outgrown errors.New.
